messages.subject: problems with volume of additional prediction observations
messages.subject_clean: problems with volume of additional prediction observations
messages.body_plain:
I have noticed that when I add a certain number of "NA" observations in order to generate predictions, that INLA seems to be crashing and refusing even to fit the non-NA data.

Reproducible example below. There is no problem with the toy example when "n" is set to 1e3 or 1e4 observations.  However, at 1e5 observations, the number of additional, prediction-only rows seems to exceed what INLA is prepared to accept and it crashes.

I am using Windows, version 18.07.  Not using Pardiso.  Windows 10, Windows R Open 5.3.1 with MKL.

It's not clear to me if this is an intended result (e.g., INLA will accept only so many additional prediction-only rows by design) or a bug (e.g., this is unintended and something that would be fixed if disclosed).

Here are the last few lines of code in verbose mode and the error message:

----------------------------
Numerical integration of hyperparameters:
Maximum number of function evaluations [100000]
Relative error ....................... [1e-005]
Absolute error ....................... [1e-006]
To stabilise the numerical optimisation:
Minimum value of the -Hessian [-1.#INF]

Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() :
  The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully.
  If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.
----------------------------

Here is the toy example that reproduces the problem, with what I hope are helpful comments:

----------------------------

### load packages

require(INLA)
require(tidyverse)
require(doParallel)

### define and gather variables

n <- 1e5 ### works fine with 1e3 and 1e4 observations; crashes with 1e5 observations

b1 <- rnorm(n)
b2 <- rpois(n, 1)
b3 <- sample(c("x1", "x2", "c3"), size=n, replace=TRUE)

z1 <- as.character(sample(seq.int <http://seq.int>(1:50), size=n, replace=TRUE))
z2 <- as.character(sample(seq.int <http://seq.int>(1:500), size=n, replace=TRUE))
z3 <- as.character(sample(seq.int <http://seq.int>(1:1000), size=n, replace=TRUE))

y <- as.integer(sample(c(0,1), size=n, replace=TRUE))

df <- as_data_frame(cbind(
  b1,
  b2, b3, z1, z2, z3,
  y
))

df$y <- as.numeric(df$y)
df$b1 <- as.numeric(df$b1)
df$b2 <- as.numeric(df$b2) ### data to be fit

### create prediction set with NA and combine with original data set

y.pred <- sample_n(df, size=2*n, replace=TRUE)
y.pred <- sample_n(df, size=n, replace=TRUE)
y.pred$y <- NA

final.df <- dplyr::bind_rows(df, y.pred)
final.df$y <- as.numeric(final.df$y) ### data to be fit combined with prediction-only rows

### fit data, but no additional data to predict

fit.1 <- inla(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 +
                f(z1, model="iid") + f(z2, model="iid") + f(z3, model="iid")
              ,
              family="binomial",
              data=df,
              control.compute = list(config=TRUE),
              control.predictor =  list(compute=TRUE, link=1),
              control.inla = list(strategy='gaussian'),
              control.fixed = list(mean=0, prec=1),
              blas.num.threads = detectCores(logical = FALSE),
              num.threads = detectCores(logical = FALSE),
              verbose=TRUE)

### fit data, but include additional data to predict

fit.2 <- inla(y ~ b1 + b2 + b3 +
                f(z1, model="iid") + f(z2, model="iid") + f(z3, model="iid")
              ,
              family="binomial",
              data=final.df,
              control.compute = list(config=TRUE),
              control.predictor =  list(compute=TRUE, link=1),
              control.inla = list(strategy='gaussian'),
              control.fixed = list(mean=0, prec=1),
              blas.num.threads = detectCores(logical = FALSE),
              num.threads = detectCores(logical = FALSE),
              verbose=TRUE)

--------------------------

with n set to 1e3, 1e4, or 1e5, fit.1 runs fine every time.  fit.2 runs fine with n set to 1e3 and 1e4, but crashes at 1e5.

-------------------

Thanks,
Jonathan

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] problems with volume of additional prediction observations
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] problems with volume of additional prediction observations
messages.body_plain:
This runs fine with me, and I guess the problem is due to lack of MEM.
you might solve it using num.threads=1, maybe, but...

When you do such many predictions, INLA, by default, consider them as
well, as part of the model allthough they are not providing information
to the parameter estimatation. Unless the number of NA's are small,
this is not a very efficient way to do it as the cost grows faster than
O(n).

Another approach, that we are using more and more, is to sample from
the (INLA-)fitted model using

	inla.posterior.sample

see the help page for info. there is also a function, which can help to
estimate any statstic(s) of the samples, ie, your predictions.

This would scale much much better, and would solve your problem.

let me know how this goes

H

I'm performing a BYM model with Zero-inflated Poisson, with this formula:

formula.zip <- Y ~ 1 + f(ZBS,  model="bym", graph=LDN.adj,
                hyper=list(prec.unstruct=list(prior="gaussian",param=c(0,1)),
                           prec.spatial=list(prior="gaussian",param=c(0,1))))

The model looks this way:

mod.zip1 <- inla(formula.zip,family="zeroinflatedpoisson0",
                 data=data.navarra, offset = log(E),
                 control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),verbose=TRUE)

However, when I run the model I get this error message:

Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed()

Rerunning with verbose=TRUE, this was reported:

messages.body_plain:
H,

Thank you for this.  I switched to a higher memory machine and the examples I provided below started working; that said, INLA does still crash when the number of NAs is notably larger than the number of successes in the binomial.  I also actually find the time penalty from including the NA prediction observations to be incredibly modest, at least with only a few “iid” columns as hyperparameters.  So ideally this option would still be available, particularly to check the accuracy of sampled predictions, although with a very low number of noted successes the addition of too many NAs may just make the model too unstable.

I do have a question about using the sampler.eval function.

I have been using this function and agree it is very useful, particularly when you wish to summarize or otherwise manipulate the posterior predictive distribution, as working with samples is much easier than densities.  But while the sampler.eval function perfectly matches up fixed effect coefficients with both existing and new observations (presumably because the coefficient can just be multiplied times the respective values for each observation in the chosen data set for prediction), I am having trouble getting the correct matchups between a prediction data set and the coefficients / intercepts for the IID effects, probably because those are of course ordinarily just added to the linear predictor rather than multiplied times some reference value in each row.

Do you have any ideas on how to “tell” the sampler.eval function which iid value it needs to use in a given row for a prediction?  Perhaps some sort of join / merge of the sampled RE coefficients into the prediction data set and then the correct value for each row can just be added to the predictor?  One can of course do all of this manually (e.g., https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic112.html) but that seems to defeat the intended convenience of the sampler.eval function.

To illustrate (I hope), in a model of inla(y ~ x1,data=df,family=”binomial”) both the inla.linear.predictor and the sampler.eval function will easily get the same values to a few decimal places, because to inla.posterior.sampler.eval the function for the necessary formula is just “Intercept + x1*df$x1”, which is easily applied to each row of the prediction set.  However, in a model of inla(y ~ x1 + f(z1, model=’iid’), data=df, family=’binomial’) the function I find myself using is “Intercept + x1*df$x1 + z1” and the evaluator seems to have no idea which value of z1 is appropriate for each row.  It appears to just recycle values from the vector of intercepts for z1.  To be clear, I completely understand why it is confused, because my formula doesn’t tell it what value of z1 to use, but I would appreciate any suggestions on how to address this within the convenient evaluator framework, so that iid effects can be keyed to a particular row for predictions.  None of my ideas have worked.

Thanks,

Jonathan

This runs fine with me, and I guess the problem is due to lack of MEM.

you might solve it using num.threads=1, maybe, but...

When you do such many predictions, INLA, by default, consider them as

well, as part of the model allthough they are not providing information

to the parameter estimatation. Unless the number of NA's are small,

this is not a very efficient way to do it as the cost grows faster than

O(n).

Another approach, that we are using more and more, is to sample from

the (INLA-)fitted model using

                inla.posterior.sample

see the help page for info. there is also a function, which can help to

estimate any statstic(s) of the samples, ie, your predictions.

This would scale much much better, and would solve your problem.

let me know how this goes

H

messages.body_plain:
maybe this example will help.

H

***************

n = 100
z1 = rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)
eta = 0.5 + z1
p = exp(eta)/(exp(eta) + 1)
size = 100
y = rbinom(n, size = size, prob=p)
df = data.frame(y, x1, z1 = 1:n)

r = inla(y ~ x1+f(z1, model="iid",
                  hyper = list(
                      prec = list(
                          prior = "pc.prec",
                          param = c(2, 0.01)))),
         data=df,
         family="binomial",
         Ntrials = size,
         control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE),
         control.compute = list(config=TRUE))

x = inla.posterior.sample(1000, r)

fun = function(df) {
    Intercept + z1
}

xf = inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun, x, df = df)
plot(rowMeans(xf), eta)
abline(0, 1)

n = 100

eta = 0.5 + z1

y = rbinom(n, size = size, prob=p)

r = inla(y ~ 1+f(z1, model="iid",

                  hyper = list(
                      prec = list(
                          prior = "pc.prec",
                          param = c(2, 0.01)))),
         data=df,
         family="binomial",
         Ntrials = size,
         control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE),
         control.compute = list(config=TRUE))

x = inla.posterior.sample(1000, r)

fun = function(df) {
    Intercept + z1
}

xf = inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun, x, df = df)

par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
plot(rowMeans(xf), eta)
abline(0, 1)
plot(rowMeans(xf), r$summary.linear.predictor[, "mean"])
abline(0, 1)

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to run an SVC model with besag random effects with inlabru.

#### graph
nb1 <- poly2nb(shapefile_name, row.names=shapefile_name$grid_id)
nb2INLA("nb1.graph", nb1)
g <- inla.read.graph("nb1.graph")

#### formula
form1 <- count ~ -1 +
    alpha_i(map=grid_id1, model="besag", graph=g, constr=FALSE, scale.model=TRUE,
        hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01)))) +
    epsilon_i(map=grid_id2, log_hrs, model="besag", graph=g, constr=FALSE, scale.model=TRUE,
        hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01)))) +
    tau_i(map=grid_id3, std_yr, model="besag", graph=g, constr=FALSE, scale.model=TRUE,
        hyper = list(prec = list( prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01)))) +
    circle_k(map=circle_id, model="iid", n=n_circs,
        hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01))))

#### function call
out1 <-  bru(form1, family="nbinomial", data=modeling_data,
                  options=list(control.predictor=list(compute=F, link=1),
                  control.compute=list(cpo=T, config=T),
                  control.inla = list(strategy="adaptive",
                                 int.strategy="auto"),
                  num.threads=2,
                  verbose=T))

#### error
I get this error related to knowing the number of grid cells:

"Error in if (n.from.graph <= 0) { : argument is of length zero"

#### question
I see there is an n argument for the iid effect. Is there an analogous arg for a besag model? Or should I just do this in straight inla?

Thanks! Tim

Hi,
Yes, please try it with an explicit “n” argument in inlabru.
If that doesn’t work, then using “plain inla” is what I’d recommend at the moment; we’re working on full support for all inla models in inlabru, but we haven’t done proper testing with graph based models yet.

If you’re able to turn this into a reproducible code example and report as an inlabru github issue that would help us sort these issues out; those of us who work on the inlabru code tend not to work on graph models, so testing is difficult without help from users!

Finn

messages.subject: How to deal with area fractions in spatial analysis?
messages.subject_clean: How to deal with area fractions in spatial analysis?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all

I have a question om modeling strategy:

My data are basically areas of located farms. That is for each observed location I know the magnitude of an area around it, but not the shape. Actually, the observed areas are not exactly what I want. Rather I should have the fraction of farm area relative to all area. The problem is how to extract this information.

A first idea is to take a square of area A around each observation point, and take the sum of observed areas within the square relative to A as an approximate fraction. In turn the fraction or its log can be used as observation. Another approach could be to translate to binomial data and let 1-s weighted with farm area fraction and 0-s weighted with 1-fraction be the INLA-observations. The appropriate size of A need to be guessed for suitable smoothing.

Another idea is to utilize the mesh. Each node of the inner part of the mesh can be taken as observation nodes where the non-farm area of the surrounding triangles are located. The data should then be considered binomial as above. I see that the calculation of the non-farm area for each node is somewhat technical, but more precise locations of the non-farm area can posssibly be obtained in this way. The range parameter of the SPDE need to be guessed for suitable smoothing. I do not necessarily need precise information in areas with no farmland, but in these cases I might just as well impute NAs.

What do you think? Are there other altternatives?

best
Øyvind

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] How to deal with area fractions in spatial analysis?
messages.body_plain:
You are right, Finn. I am not modelling the farm sizes.

The object of the analysis is the grain crop yield per ha and the impact of distances to centers. I observe areas of crop land, areas with grain crop, and total grain yield for specific farm locations. I also observe center location for calculation of straight distance to nearest center. The hypotheses from economics is that longer distance means lower profit per ha, lower input intensity and lower yields. The problem from causal analysis is that low fractions of crop land in general and crop land used for grain in particular (relative to all land) are possible confounders for both distance to center and yield per ha. One should at least try to correct for this in order to find the causal effect of distance.

I guess there might be similar cases in disease mapping when the concentration of people affects the infection rates? One would then need not only observation of infections but also non-infections?

Øyvind

messages.body_plain:
Will submit bug to inlabru git repo.  But, in case it is useful to others in the mean time, looks like there were two issues.

First, don't name your graph 'g' when using bru(). It breaks when you do this. I think because there is a function named g within inlabru.

Second, looks like, even when using a different graph name, bru doesn't know what to do with the second weighting variable argument that is necessary in the model formula when you are specifying a 'besag' spatially varying coefficient model.

Best, Tim

Reproducible example:

# start -----------------
library(INLA)
library(inlabru)
library(spdep)
data(columbus)

# adj matrix
g <- W <- as(as_dgRMatrix_listw(nb2listw(col.gal.nb)),
             "CsparseMatrix")

# poly id
columbus$idx<-1:nrow(columbus)

# inla works
form<- CRIME ~ INC + HOVAL + f(idx, model="besag", graph=g)
inla1 <-  inla(form, data=columbus)
summary(inla1)

# bru breaks when graph is named 'g'
form <- CRIME ~ INC + HOVAL + f(idx, model="besag", graph=g)
bru1 <-  bru(form, data=columbus, family="gaussian")

# bru works when graph is not named 'g'
form <- CRIME ~ INC + HOVAL + location(map=idx,
                                       model="besag", graph=W)
bru2 <-  bru(form, data=columbus, family="gaussian")
summary(bru2)

# inla doesn't work after bru is called with graph 'g'
form<- CRIME ~ INC + HOVAL + f(idx, model="besag", graph=g)
inla2 <-  inla(form, data=columbus)

# start over ---------------
rm(list=ls())
library(INLA)
library(inlabru)
library(spdep)
data(columbus)

# adj matrix
g <- W <- as(as_dgRMatrix_listw(nb2listw(col.gal.nb)),
             "CsparseMatrix")

# poly id
columbus$idx<-1:nrow(columbus)

# inla works for spatially varying slopes
form<- CRIME ~ INC + HOVAL + f(idx, INC, model="besag", graph=g)
inla3 <-  inla(form, data=columbus)
summary(inla3)

# bru doesn't work with SVC, even with graph not named 'g'
form <- CRIME ~ INC + HOVAL + f(idx, INC, model="besag", graph=W)
bru3 <-  bru(form, data=columbus, family="gaussian")

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inlabru besag spatial model syntax
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

yes, in the current inlabru version there is a "g" function with
similar purpose as the INLA::f function that will interfere with
component naming. I believe the experimental backend changes will
remove this issue.

Instead of specifying f(..., weight), the idea in inlabru is to
include it explicitly in the formula expression, and the formula is
distinct from the model component specification (but in simple cases,
the formula is inferred from the component spec).
In the absence of other bugs, the model would be written as follows:

comp <- ~ INC + HOVAL + field(map = idx, model="besag", graph=W,
n=the_graph_size)
form <- CRIME ~ INC + HOVAL + field * INC
bru3 <-  bru(comp, like(data=columbus, family="gaussian", formula = form))

(I suspect this version will also fail, but a test case for that would
be very welcome!)

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to deal with area fractions in spatial analysis?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] How to deal with area fractions in spatial analysis?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Finn.

As presumed, I am slightly off the broad track of INLA-SPDE modelling. Anyway, I guess nothing but INLA-SPDE will carrry me through.

Some more explicit reasoning: Assume some resource is uniformly spread in space, and that centers are formed to gather a certain amount of that resource with a minimum of transportation costs. Centers will then arise in a triangular grid. Distance between centers --- and average distance to center alike --- will then depend on the concentration of the resource. If the study variable possibly depends both on the concentration and the distance to center, a measure of concentration is required in the causal regression model. In some way it can be deduced from the observations of the resource. The question is how. A first point to note: I have no interest in low-range SPDE fields of concentration. These will not affect center locations to large extent. It is the long-range fields that will. Moreover the relevant range should be sufficiently large to cover 3-4 centers on average. Else the correlation between concentration and distance will be weak.

This analysis has implications for the modelling. Either I could calculate concentration within squares covering the neighborhoods of approximately 4 centers for each observation, and take these as covariates, or I could measure concentration  in some more detail and extract the relevant information with a sufficiently long-range SPDE-field.The covariate approach makes the model smaller. I would in any case need an SPDE-field for the residuals of the regression. 2-3 additional fields for the regressors plus stocastic regression parameters lead to a pretty large model.

Preliminary conclusion is that my first proposal is simplest and preferrable.

best
Øyvind

torsdag 11. oktober 2018 15.19.38 UTC+2 skrev Finn Lindgren følgende:
> I see. Rereading the original message with this in mind, it seems to em you have a very tricky problem, in that you need information about area fractions at locations where it wasn’t measures, and the locations where you do have measurements might themselves be confounded with those fractions (depending on how the spatial observation design was made). The idea of modelling the fraction (which might be less confounded than the absolute areas) as a spatial field seems like a reasonable compromise to me. However, I wasn’t able to follow the details of what your idea for how to do that; perhaps that’s because the area measurements lack information about the locations where you don’t have measurements?
>
> Finn
>
> On 11 Oct 2018, at 14:08, Øyvind <oeyh...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > You are right, Finn. I am not modelling the farm sizes.
> >
> > The object of the analysis is the grain crop yield per ha and the impact of distances to centers. I observe areas of crop land, areas with grain crop, and total grain yield for specific farm locations. I also observe center location for calculation of straight distance to nearest center. The hypotheses from economics is that longer distance means lower profit per ha, lower input intensity and lower yields. The problem from causal analysis is that low fractions of crop land in general and crop land used for grain in particular (relative to all land) are possible confounders for both distance to center and yield per ha. One should at least try to correct for this in order to find the causal effect of distance.
> >
> > I guess there might be similar cases in disease mapping when the concentration of people affects the infection rates? One would then need not only observation of infections but also non-infections?
> >
> > Øyvind
> >
> > torsdag 11. oktober 2018 13.41.54 UTC+2 skrev Finn Lindgren følgende:
> > > Hi,
> > >
> > > Can you clarify what you’re observing, as I get the impression that it’s not the farm sizes that you’re modelling, but rather that the farm sizes are relevant to what you’re observing (e.g. if the observations are something like “number of trees”). How the farm sizes would be used depends entirely on why they are relevant!
> > >
> > > Finn
> > >
> > > On 11 Oct 2018, at 12:12, Øyvind <oeyh...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > Dear all
> > > >
> > > > I have a question om modeling strategy:
> > > >
> > > > My data are basically areas of located farms. That is for each observed location I know the magnitude of an area around it, but not the shape. Actually, the observed areas are not exactly what I want. Rather I should have the fraction of farm area relative to all area. The problem is how to extract this information.
> > > >
> > > > A first idea is to take a square of area A around each observation point, and take the sum of observed areas within the square relative to A as an approximate fraction. In turn the fraction or its log can be used as observation. Another approach could be to translate to binomial data and let 1-s weighted with farm area fraction and 0-s weighted with 1-fraction be the INLA-observations. The appropriate size of A need to be guessed for suitable smoothing.
> > > >
> > > > Another idea is to utilize the mesh. Each node of the inner part of the mesh can be taken as observation nodes where the non-farm area of the surrounding triangles are located. The data should then be considered binomial as above. I see that the calculation of the non-farm area for each node is somewhat technical, but more precise locations of the non-farm area can posssibly be obtained in this way. The range parameter of the SPDE need to be guessed for suitable smoothing. I do not necessarily need precise information in areas with no farmland, but in these cases I might just as well impute NAs.
> > > >
> > > > What do you think? Are there other altternatives?

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Precision
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Yes, virtually all numerics is safer when done closer to the “source”. Transforming the density representation is always a lossy operation (since it’s essentially a finite evaluation of a spline approximation), so it’s safer to not do a whole chain of such transformation, but instead calculate the desired quantities directly from the representation used in the construction of the inla-approximation itself.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] exact log Marginal likelihood
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

for the intrinsic models, like RW1, RW2, BESAG, etc, the determinant of
the precision matrix's part of the normalizing constant is not
included. |A|^*  is the 'generalized' determinant, like the determinant
of the nonsingular part of A, or simply the product of all non-zero
eigenvalues.

For DIC, WAIC, this constant is not needed, only if you happen to
compare marginal likelihood with and without a RW2 term, f.ex.

H

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inlabru besag spatial model syntax
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your help, Finn.  For others, here is a reproducible example that should work. By the way, I am using the columbus data from spdep, because it is widely available and can be used to demonstrate the syntax, not because it is the correct thing to do.

### CAR spatially varying coefficient SVC model with inlabru ###

# libraries
suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(require(INLA)))
suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(require(brinla)))
suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(require(inlabru)))
suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(require(spdep)))
suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(require(rgdal)))
suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(require(sf)))

# data
data(columbus)

# weights matrix
weights1 <- as(as_dgRMatrix_listw(nb2listw(col.gal.nb)), "CsparseMatrix")

# region index
columbus$index1<-1:nrow(columbus)

# number regions
n_weights1 <- max(columbus$index1)

# make bru components
comp1 <- ~
  random_intercepts(map=index1, model="besag", graph=weights1, scale.model=T) +
  random_inc_slopes(map=index1, model="besag", graph=weights1, scale.model=T) +
  Intercept

# make bru formula
form1 <- CRIME ~ -1 + random_intercepts + random_inc_slopes * INC + Intercept

# get bru results
bru1 <- bru(comp1, like(data=columbus, family="gaussian", formula=form1))

# access results
bru1$summary.fixed
head(bru1$summary.random$random_intercepts)
head(bru1$summary.random$random_inc_slopes)
bri.hyperpar.summary(bru1)

# plot results
plot(bru1, "Intercept")
plot(bru1, "random_intercepts")
plot(bru1, "random_inc_slopes")

# map SVCs
columbus_shape <- as(readOGR(system.file("shapes/columbus.shp", package="spData")[1]), "sf")
columbus_shape$rand_slopes_mean <- bru1$summary.random$random_inc_slopes$mean
columbus_shape$rand_slopes_sd <- bru1$summary.random$random_inc_slopes$sd
plot(columbus_shape["rand_slopes_mean"])
plot(columbus_shape["rand_slopes_sd"])

messages.subject: CAR as a linear combination
messages.body_plain:
Hi R-INLA users,

I'm trying to fit a hierarchical model where the latent field is comprised of a CAR component which is a sum of (correlated) random variables,

y ~ z + e,

where y denotes my response, e a random effect and z=beta_1*x_1+beta_2*x_2+...+beta_k*x_k is determined by a CAR model.

I've found that if k=1 (z=beta*x), it's possible by using f(idx,x,model="bym(for instance)",...). Is there a way to specify this model and to get estimates of beta_1, beta_2,..., and beta_k? I appreciate your help in advance.

Best,
Roman.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] CAR as a linear combination
messages.body_plain:
so (beta_1, beta_2, ..., beta_k) comes from a CAR model? and you
observe

y_i = \sum_j beta_j*x_ij + e_i,

say, or the rhs is the linear predictor for another likeilhood.

you can use the 'A' in the control.predictor to construct this.

the A-matrix, constructs a new linear predictor, eta*, that is

	eta* = A %*% eta

and eta is give by a formula, and eta* connects to the data. See

http://www.r-inla.org/models/tools#TOC-Models-where-the-response-data-depends-on-linear-combinations-of-the-linear-predictor-or-the-sum-of-fixed-and-random-effects
-

so you see that if you define (assuming 'e' is not the 'likelihood')

	eta = [beta_1, ..., beta_k, e_1, ...., e_n],

you can define

A = [ x_11, x_12, x_13, ..., x_1k, 1, 0, 0, ..., 0 ]
    [ x_21, x_22, x_23, ..., x_2k, 0, 1, 0, ..., 0 ]
      :

where A is n x (k+n) matrix

and then use the formula

	y ~ -1 + f(idx, model="besag", constr=F) + f(idx2)

where

idx = c(1:k, rep(NA,n))
idx2 = c(rep(NA,k),1:n)

and add

	inla(..., control.predictor = list(A = A))

start with a simple example and make sure you get it right, and
expand...

Best
H

messages.body_plain:
The z_i cannot simultaneously be a deterministic function of the betas and have CAR structure. Do you rather want the _expectation_ of the z to take that linear combination form, conditionally on the betas? What model do you want for the betas? Does beta_k refer to an entire field, or is each beta_k a scalar?
I would highly recommend spelling out the details of the desired model in precise probabilistic terms instead of pseudo R notation!

Finn

Let (y_1, y_2, ..., y_n) be a set of observed counts modelled as Poisson random variables conditionally independent given their expected value, E ( y_i ) = mu_i:

y_i | mu_i ~ Poi ( mu_i ).

Let's assume that

log( mu_i ) = z_i + e_i,

where (z_1, z_2, ..., z_n) is an unknown (latent) field with a CAR structure and (e_1, e_2, ..., e_n) are realizations of a random effect (error terms).

If I also have measurements at the same level than y_i, namely x_i1, x_i2, ..., x_ik, which I would like to link with the mean of the latent variable z_i :

E ( z_i ) = beta_i1*x_i1 + beta_i2*x_i2 + ... + beta_ik*x_ik,

where (x_i1, x_i2, ..., x_ik) follow a multivariate normal distribution and (beta_i1, beta_i2, ..., beta_ik) are a set of parameters.

Is there a way to specify this relationship using the inla function in order to estimate (beta_1, beta_2, ..., beta_k)? When k=1 (z_i = beta_1*x_i1) it's possible by using f(id, x_1, model="besag",...). In this terms, I'd like something like f(id, (x_1+x_2+ ... + x_k), model="besag",...).

Best,
Roman.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] CAR as a linear combination
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Since the beta&x only appear in the expectation for z, I should suggest simply splitting z into its expectation and random variation, where the random variation is a zero mean CAR model. This is how we normally build models of this type. The inla formula could look something like this:
y ~ x1 + x2 + f(zindex, model=“besag”)
This would result in parameters beta1 and beta2 multiplying x1 and x2, and the combined effect would look like what you describe.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Aha, so you want each beta to be a spatial CAR field of it's own, and
on top of that add CAR variability?
The same principle applies; the z-variability can have an f() of its
own (seems it's a BYM model you want for that, with CAR+independent
noise?), with zero mean, and each beta can have its own f():

For example,
  y ~ f(beta1, x1, model="besag") + f(beta2, x2, model="besag") + f(z,
model="bym")
with family="possion", so that E(y_i) = exp(eta_i) would define a
model where at each location,
 \eta_i = beta1_i x1_i + beta2_i x2_i + z_i

If the number of beta-fields is dynamic or large, that becomes tedious
to spell out, and you get one hyperparameter for each term as well,
but it seems to be what you're looking for.

Finn

messages.subject: Getting predictions on natural scale for lognormal family
messages.subject_clean: Getting predictions on natural scale for lognormal family
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
If I fit a model like
m1 <- inla(y ~x, family = "poisson", control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1))
(A log-link Poisson GLM)
Then m1$summary.fitted.values will be on the count scale and m1$summary.linear.predictor will be on the log scale.
But if I do
m1 <- inla(y ~x, family = "lognormal", control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1))
Both the linear predictor and the fitted values will be on the log scale.
Is there a way I can get predictions on the natural scale for a lognormal model?
My motivation is that I want to account for retransformation bias when calculating predictions (and the CIs) for y.
ie ln(y) = a + bx + error;
so predictions for y need to account for the error, so:
y = exp(a + bx)*exp(error)
Thanks
Chris

messages.body_plain:
yes, the reason is, as you say, that its simply just

log(y) ~ Normal(,)

so the link is the identity:

> inla.models()$likelihood$lognormal$link
[1] "default"  "identity"
>

if you want results on the exp-scale, you have to transform them
manually, like densitites with inla.tmarginal(exp, marginal), or just
doing exp on the quantiles, like on the linear predictor.

if you want predictions on the data-level, its easiest to use sampling,
like inla.posterior.sample() and inla.posterior.sample.eval(), as we
adding new data from a given likelihood is not implemented.

Best
H

messages.subject: Prediction changes the estimates! why?
messages.body_plain:
So I was working with some time series and I found that if I fitted 20 years of data I was getting certain estimates but if I was fitting 19 years of data and wanted to predict the last year of data, then the estimates for all the years differed a little. I did not think much of it, but when i included the space component to my model then I got things drastically different.

So I thought it was my code.

To figure out what went wrong I started a the beginning and decided to look at the example in the R-INAL webpage

Here is the code I ran:

## Load the data
require(INLA)
data(Tokyo)
summary(Tokyo)

Tokyo$y1 <- Tokyo$y
Tokyo$y1[300:366] <- NA

## Define the model
# all the data
formula = y ~ f(time, model="rw2", cyclic=TRUE, param=c(1,0.0001)) - 1
# partial data without the prediction part
formulapart = y[1:299] ~ f(time, model="rw2", cyclic=TRUE, param=c(1,0.0001)) - 1
# the partial data with the prediction part
formulapred = y1 ~ f(time, model="rw2", cyclic=TRUE, param=c(1,0.0001)) - 1

## The call to inca

result = inla(formula, family="binomial", Ntrials=n, data=Tokyo,
              control.predictor=list(compute=T))
resultpart = inla(formulapart, family="binomial", Ntrials=n, data=Tokyo[1:299,],
              control.predictor=list(compute=T))

# two methods of predictions
link = rep(NA, nrow(Tokyo))
link[which(is.na <http://is.na>(Tokyo$y1))] = 1
resultpred = inla(formulapred, family="binomial", Ntrials=n, data=Tokyo,
              control.predictor=list(compute=T))
resultpredL = inla(formulapred, family="binomial", Ntrials=n, data=Tokyo,
                  control.predictor=list(compute=T, link = link))

summary(result)
summary(result part)
# this two below give the same (good)
summary(resultpred)
summary(resultpredL)

cbind(result$summary.random$time[1:20,2],
      resultpart$summary.random$time[1:20,2],
      resultpred$summary.random$time[1:20,2],
      resultpredL$summary.random$time[1:20,2])

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Prediction changes the estimates! why?
messages.body_plain:
Have you checked the constraint settings for the rw2 model? When a sum-to-zero constrain is applied, it’s applied to the whole model component, so the size of the model matters; for example, a model with 20 timepoints and missing values for the last 10 is not the same model as a model that only has the first 10 timepoints.
This is an inherent issue that is particularly common when intrinsic models are used (but you’ll need to check if this is what’s happening in this particular case). To avoid that issue, look at the total prediction instead of the model component.

Finn

####################################################################
####     EXAMPLE 1  from Ruiz-Cárdenas,Krainski, and Rue (2012) ####
####################################################################

## Simulating a Poisson dynamic regression (p1814)
## (dynamic intercept and two dynamic regrressors)
## -----------------------------------------------
require(INLA)
set.seed(123456)

n <- 300
x1 <- runif(n)
x2 <- runif(n)
W0 = 0.005
W1 = 0.01
W2 <- 0.005
w0 <- rnorm(n,0,sqrt(W0))
w1 <- rnorm(n,0,sqrt(W1))
w2 <- rnorm(n,0,sqrt(W2))
y <- b0 <- b1 <- b2 <- numeric(n)
b0[1] <- 3 + w0[1]
b1[1] <- 0 + w1[1]
b2[1] <- 0 + w2[1]
for (t in 2:n){
  b0[t] <- b0[t-1] + w0[t]
  b1[t] <- b1[t-1] + w1[t]
  b2[t] <- b2[t-1] + w2[t]
}
y <- rpois(n,exp(b0 + b1*x1 + b2*x2))
y1 <- y
y1[276:300] <- NA

data <- data.frame(x1, x2, y, y1)

# defining indices for rw1 coefficients
# -------------------------------------
id <- 1:n    # indices for beta_0
id1 <- 1:n   # indices for beta_1
id2 <- 1:n   # indices for beta_2

# formulating the model
# ---------------------
# formulation with default hyperprior for all the data
formula <- y ~ f(id, model="rw1",constr=F) +
  f(id1, x1, model="rw1",constr=F) +
  f(id2, x2, model="rw1",constr=F) -1
# formulation with default hyperprior for all the data[1:275] and NA[276:300]
link = rep(NA, nrow(data))
link[which(is.na(data$y1))] = 1
formulaPRED <- y1 ~ f(id, model="rw1",constr=F) +
  f(id1, x1, model="rw1",constr=F) +
  f(id2, x2, model="rw1",constr=F) -1

# call to fit the model
# ---------------------
# Fitting all 300 data points
r <- inla(formula, family="poisson", data = data.frame(id,id1,id2,data),
          control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE))

# Fitting the first 274 and have the last 25
rPRED <- inla(formulaPRED, family="poisson", data = data.frame(id,id1,id2,data),
          control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, link = link))

# Compare the output of the non-predicted part
intercepts <- cbind(r$summary.random$id[1:20,2],
      rPRED$summary.random$id[1:20,2])
betahat1s <- cbind(r$summary.random$id1[1:20,2],
      rPRED$summary.random$id1[1:20,2])
betahat2s <- cbind(r$summary.random$id2[1:20,2],
      rPRED$summary.random$id2[1:20,2])
comparison <- data.frame(intercepts, betahat1s, betahat2s)
colnames(comparison) <- c("B0hat","B0 w/ Pred",
                          "B1hat","B1 w/ Pred",
                          "B1hat","B1 w/ Pred")
comparison

I simulated n=300. fitted a simple RW1 dynamic model with all the data, and then with the data where I replaced the last 25 y by NA to have it predict. and when i compare the betas for the first 20 datapoint at the beginning of the model, they are not the same for any of them…. and those should not change since they are not part of the predicted portion

thank you for your help in trying to get the same betas estimates for the non-prediction portion, with and without prediction

SAB

Thank you for your response.

here is how I came to think that something was not right with how INLA was predicting...

I am working on a model quite complex. R-INLA does a great job at fitting the model. However, I was given additional data and wanted to check how prediction was performing. and it is when i notice things started to be very off when i was considering space in addition than just time. When only time is in question the difference between the two cases (the original data and the data plus the NA of the new data to run the check) is minimal and I could live with it.

But exactly same model with the exception of three covariates and BYM space component and now things falls apart when I try to predict

Here is the great fit for one area when i am not doing prediction (the wiggling is due to the presence of the other covariate effects):

But with prediction in for just one sequence

Not only you can see that the prediction part is completely the wrong way, but it changed the model before that drastically.... So, i do understand that numerical approximations are not exact, and I was not troubled when I first tried to predict with just time but when the model is complex it seems to go beyond the mere approximation error.

Or maybe the errors are cumulative, making prediction in the case of complex models not feasible?

But the part that was the most troubling me what that it changed the model itself so much when i try to predict that it rendered the fitting part not good anymore.

Hence, my reaching out to figure out on more simple example why I was seeing the exact same behavior or if it was something that i was missing when I was programming even a simple dynamic model.

Again thank you,

SAB.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Prediction changes the estimates! why?
messages.body_plain:
the changes in the figures you show is not due to rounding errors.
if could be the same error as in the prev example: setting some
observations to NA, also removes from from the fitting, hence all
results changes. this was the case in the prev example.

you get also predictions from where you have data. it might be a
confusion about termonology that is the root here.

H

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] CAR Model
messages.body_plain:
There's some confusion here."E" is used for the poisson model, but since you have proportions, it's not really relevant.
If you knew the total that your percentage was computed from you would rather be looking at a Binomial observation model, where Normals specifies the total possible counts.

If the total counts weren't recorded, then you'll need to make simplifying assumptions/approximations.
 If the total count was different for each observation and that information wasn't recorded, then you won't be able to model the true observation model. But if the total count was the same for all, but still unknown, then you might consider a Beta distribution as you observation family, directly on the percentages.

Finn

messages.subject: Incorporating Survey Design in CAR model in R INLA

messages.body_plain:
I have survey data at individual level, with PSU (primary sampling unit), Strata( subnational unit and rural/urban) and survey weights. In addition, I have levels of education for education for each participant correlated over time.

I need to specify a small area estimation model(SAE), that accounts for the survey design, has both space, time and space-time terms. The output should be subnational unit with s.e and CIs.

I have previous experience of doing SAE using aggregated data that do not have a particular survey design. The approach has been based on the following example from  Spatial and Spatio-temporal Bayesian models with R-INLA <https://sites.google.com/a/r-inla.org/stbook/>

formula.intIV<- y ~ f(ID.area,model="bym",graph=Georgia.adj) +
  f(ID.year,model="rw2") +
  f(ID.year1,model="iid") +
  f(ID.area.int,model="besag", graph=Georgia.adj,group=ID.year.int,control.group=list(model="rw2"))

mod.intIV <- inla(formula.intIV,family="poisson",data=data,E=E,
                  control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
                  control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))

How to adapt this formulation to individual data and incorporate the survey design?

Thanks
Peter

In contrast to frequentistic estimators, a Bayesian model requires an explicit probabilistic construction. Finn

messages.body_plain:
The below is the information available for survey design:

Enumeration areas (EA) are selected, using a two-stage sample design from a national sampling frame. In addition, the sampling frame is divided into subgroups/strata that are as homogeneous as possible using subnational unit and by rural/urban within the subnational unit.

In the first stage of selection, the primary sampling units (PSUs) are selected with probability proportional to size within each stratum.  The PSUs are typically census enumeration areas (EAS).  The PSU forms the survey cluster. In the second stage, a complete household listing is conducted in each of the selected clusters. Following the listing of the households a fixed number of households (about 25) is selected by equal probability systematic sampling in the selected cluster.

Sampling weights are adjustment factors applied to each case in tabulations to adjust for differences in probability of selection and interview between cases in a sample, due to either design or happenstance and differential response rates are also made.

In my data I have the PSU, the subnational unit and the survey weights

Peter

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the details!

It's not clear to me that the "sampling weights" need to be used here.
If you model all the unknowns (i.e. the non-observed households that
could _potentially_ have been observed) and the sampling scheme
doesn't depend on the observed quantities, than those weights are only
needed by certain frequentistic estimators.
However, if your model is only built on the aggregated PSU level (or
the sampling scheme depends on observables, directly or indirectly),
then yes, they do need to be considered.
But you'll need to decide how to incorporate them in, as describing
the entire sampling scheme isn't really feasible in R-INLA.

I'm not a SAE expert, but I believe the analogue to the frequentistic
approximations is to use the weights as multipliers on the
log-likelihoods?
This can be done with
  inla(..., weights = ...)

>From ?inla :

weights: Fixed (optional) weights parameters of the likelihood, so the
          log-likelihood[i] is changed into
          weights[i]*log-likelihood[i]. Default value is rep(1,
          n.data). Due to the danger of mis-interpreting the results
          (see below), this option is DISABLED by default. You can
          enable this option for the rest of your ‘R’ session, doing
          ‘inla.setOption(enable.inla.argument.weights=TRUE)’. WARNING:
          The normalizing constant for the likelihood is NOT
          recomputed, so ALL marginals (and the marginal likelihood)
          must be interpreted with great care. Possibly, you may want
          to set the prior for the hyperparameters to ‘"uniform"’ and
          the integration strategy to ‘"eb"’ to mimic a
          maximum-likelihood approach.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have some thought on using sampling weights on Bayesian models, in
particular in INLA.

The sampling weights are not the same as the weights parameter in
INLA. The weights parameter in INLA is the same as lm or glm functions
where they simply replicate that observation, in other terms in a
potential term for the likelihood,

Suppose a generic model with a parameter theta

Y|theta ~  G(y | theta)

Le y_1, y_2,...,y_N a random sample of Y, then the likelihood is defined as

L(theta) = \prod_{i = 1}^{N} g(y_i | theta )

Suppose the y_1 appears w_1 times, y_2 w_2,...,y_n w_n times and
sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j = n so the likelihood can be rewritten as

L(theta) = \prod_{i = 1}^{N} g(y_i | theta ) = \prod_{j = 1}^{n} g(y_j
| theta )^{w_j}

The w's are the weight parameter implemented in INLA. And they are
definitely not the sampling weights which usually they add up the
population size.

You could normalize the sampling weights such as they add up the
sample size and run in INLA, but you have to be in mind the you are no
longer dealing with the likelihood but with a Pseudo-Likelihood
instead, and therefore you would have the pseudo posterior. You may be
interested a paper by Savitsky and Toth (2016)
https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ejs/1468847267

There are some other approaches to sampling data, but the pseudo
posterior approach is the by far the easiest one to implement in INLA,
and it would work on your model.

I hope it helps, it would have helped me two years ago when I was
looking for dealing with the same issue. :-)

Cheers,
Leo

messages.subject: Estimating structural equations in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I am reasonably sure that I have read about INLA's capacity to estimate simultaneous equations, however I am having difficulty tracking this information down. Can anyone point me toward resources regarding implementation and estimation of simultaneous equations in INLA.

Just to offer a little context, I am interested in models similar to the one detailed in this paper (https://academic.oup.com/biostatistics/article/6/4/539/228600), which introduces a structural equation model with a CAR prior. It seems to me INLA could be used to conduct piecewise regression structural modeling and that exploiting INLA's capacity to simultaneously model multiple outcomes could be a nice way to approach this.

As the authors of the linked paper note, a spatial SEM model could be directly implemented and estimated via some flavor of MCMC; however, I am working with spatio-temporal county-level data and would rather avoid the computational costs of applying MCMC to such a large grid. Per usual, INLA would be perfect for my purposes.

So, I am wondering:

1. Assuming all variables are treated as observed, is it possible to specify and simultaneously estimate structural model in INLA?
2. Assuming 1. is possible, are there any restrictions on the distributional assumptions necessary for achieving 1.? For instance, can I arbitrarily model one endogenous variable as Poisson distributed and another as Gaussian?
3. Also, is there a way to model residual autocorrelation among endogenous variables?

Any thoughts or suggestions would be much appreciated!

Best,
Joe

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Estimating structural equations in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi Håvard,

Thank you for your response.

I am looking to do something similar to what's described in this blog post (http://rpubs.com/jebyrnes/343408), but extended to include car and ar(1) priors on some of the residuals.

For example, let's assume I have the following causal model where all variables are standard normal:

Y ~ X + Z
Z ~ X

In BRMS (a wrapper for STAN) we can estimate multivariate responses, so both equations can be estimated simultaneously. And, it appears that residual correlation between Y and Z can also be estimated. To evaluate this model, we might estimate something like:

Y ~ a1 + b1X + b2Z + e1
Z ~ a2 + b3X + e2

Y ~ Normal(mu = 0, sd = e1)
Z ~ Normal(mu = 0, sd = e2)
b[1,2,3] ~ Normal(0,2.5)
a[1,2] ~ Normal(0,5)
e[1,2] ~ half-normal(0,1)
cor(e1, e2) ~ Normal(0,1)

Could I do this in INLA?

If so, I'll complicate things a bit. I'll now assume that Y is actually a Poisson distributed count variable observed for each geographical unit in some areal grid.

And, I'll also assume that (1) I have monthly measurements of Y; (2) I have reason to think that, across time, different geographic units probably have different average levels of Y; (3) that there is probably spatial autocorrelation in levels of Y between adjacent units; and (4) that each unit's particular time trend is at least partly idiosyncratic (e.g. some may increase over time and some may decrease over time).

And, I'll also assume that Z is (1) a standard normal variable observed in each unit; (2) probably spatially correlated; (3) and I only have static observations of Z (e.g. Z does not change over time)

In INLA, I think I might model Y using something like (this is the first time I've worked with spatio-temporal models, so please forgive me if this isn't quite correct):

f_y <- Y ~ 1 + X + Z + f(unit_id, model='bym', group=month, control.group=list(model='ar1'))
mod_y <- inla(f_y, family='poisson')

And, I would model Z like this:

f_z <- Z ~ 1 + X + f(unit_id, model='besag')
mod_z <- inla(f_z, family='gaussian')

Now, because BRMS can handle (apparently) arbitrarily specified multivariate models, these models could be estimated simultaneously (i.e. as a system of structural equations).

So, I am wondering, can I do this in INLA? And, could I also estimate the residual correlation between Y and Z as in the first model?

Thanks!

Best,
Joe

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Estimating structural equations in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
The short answer is yes, as long as you can formulate the models to have conditionally independent observations given the two predictors (I.e. spatial dependence can be present in the predictor for the mean, but you can’t have dependence directly between the Poisson observations, just as in most other tools).

In “raw” inla, it’s a bit tedious to setup such models, but there are examples in the links on r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org> (sorry, no precise link where I’m at right now).
With the interface to inla in the “inlabru” package, it’s a bit easier, since there one can specify the two predictor formulas separately. In INLA, that needs to be done by setting up “NA” vectors and have all components in a single formula, with the data in a matrix, with one column per observation likelihood.

Finn
